name: garrow
author: food and the kitchen (kitchen agent)
description:
garrow v3 (direction: food and the kitchen) - A TRAY PIZZA, CUT INTO SLICES. PRIVATE; never shown to players.

CLUE = six lines. Line 1 is one topping letter and one digit 1-3, e.g. "m2". The rest is the uncut tray bake: a crust row of "#", four dough rows "##~~~mmm~~~~ooo~~~##" (cheese is "~", a crust of "##" at each end, every topping a 3-cell piece of a repeated lowercase letter, three pieces a row, at least two cheese cells between pieces, three topping letters drawn from "mpotacsb"), and a closing crust row. Trays are 30-36 characters wide. The named topping has 4-6 pieces on the tray.

ANSWER = the same picture with the knife lines drawn in: a "|" inserted straight down through every row at the same columns. Nothing else may change, so the player's only freedom is where the cuts go; the tray itself is given in the clue, which is what lets a player who has never seen a demo send a well-formed answer.

RULE (unchanged since v1 - every version has changed only what the picture says out loud): score = 1 iff (1) the answer, with every "|" deleted, is exactly the clue's dough rows (lines with no "~" - crust rows, a header, blank lines - are ignored, so the picture is strict but the trimmings are free); (2) the cuts are at the same columns in every row; (3) there are at least 4 slices and every slice is at least 3 characters wide; and (4) the number of slices holding TWO OR MORE pieces of the named topping equals the digit - where a piece the knife went through counts for the slice on BOTH sides of the cut. In the picture a halved topping is drawn as "m|mm", so "that slice got two mushrooms, and one of them is the half" is readable by eye. One clause a kid says in a breath: "two slices have two mushrooms on them - a mushroom cut in half counts for both sides."

WHY V3 EXISTS (the demo-economy pass, LADDER.md "Format shift"). v2 scored 64 % under the old 6-round / 6-demo format (one crack at round 5 after 6 demos, one 28 % partial with 2 demos). The new format gives a class ~60 probes a round for 4 rounds and a team only 3 demo requests for 7 classes, so v2's budget - two toppings, two digits, a 4-8 slice bound, and a crack that took 6 demos plus a 272-answer designed experiment - is out of reach. v3 keeps the object and the rule and cuts the class down to what one demo plus ~120 probes can carry:
  (a) ONE TOPPING, ONE DIGIT. v2 named two toppings and two digits because on v1 clues a player who had only the format and cut at random satisfied one count 25 % of the time. That is measured again here and it is no longer true: because generate() now picks, for each tray, a count that is RARE among random cuttings of it (the band below), a blind well-formed cutting scores 8.6 % (n drawn at random), 13.2 % (n=6 always), 15.4 % (n=5 always) - a foothold in the 5-30 % band the loop asks for, not a free 25 %. So the second letter and digit are gone and the clue is "m2" over a picture.
  (b) THE DEMO SHOWS THE COUNTED RELATION IN ONE LOOK. generate() keeps a tray only if it can be cut so that some counted slice holds EXACTLY TWO pieces of the named topping with one of them halved by the knife, the neighbouring slice holds just the other half, and the slices are visibly hand-cut (one at most 4 wide, and a spread of at least 5 between the widest and the thinnest). solve() renders that cutting, so every demo draws the sentence "this slice has two mushrooms, one of them cut in half, and next door has only the half" instead of leaving it to be inferred. 97 % of demos are that picture; solve() further prefers (46 % of demos) a cutting that also has a slice holding three, so that "exactly two" is visibly not the rule.
  (c) THE 4-8 SLICE BOUND IS GONE. Players' only complaint about v2 was "why four to eight?". The scorer now says only "at least four slices, each at least three wide", so the upper bound is whatever the tray allows (10-12) and demos run 4-9 slices. The witness table stayed clean: equal-width slices still score 0.00 % because generate() rejects any count that ANY equal cutting of that tray achieves, for every n from 4 up to width//3.
  (d) THE TRAY READS AS FOOD. Cheese is now "~" instead of ".", the crust is two columns thick at each end and a solid row above and below, and toppings are 3 cells wide with three of them a row (v2: 2 cells, 4-5 a row). Fewer, bigger pieces on a textured base; no labels or legends. The judge scored v2's object 2/5 ("a bordered dot grid does not read as pizza until it is cut") - a "~~~mmm~~~ooo~~~" tray with a thick crust is the best that is available without markers.
  (e) THE SEVERED DECOY STILL DIES IN DEMO 1. v1's run was eaten by "severed = digit + c" holding on four of five demos. generate() requires the kept witness to have severed(x) != k, and because the counted slice of the demo holds exactly two with one halved, "slices with two WHOLE pieces" and "slices the topping touches at all" cannot come to k either. Rival readings of a demo picture: 97 % of demos leave none of severed / whole-pairs / touched-at-all / two-of-any-one-topping / number-of-cuts equal to the digit.

MEASURED WITNESS TABLE (500 fresh clues, seeds 100000-100499; a strategy "builds" an answer by searching up to 400 well-formed cuttings for one satisfying its own law, then is scored by the real scorer; "built" is how often such a cutting was found at all).
  true rule (solve)                                 100.00 %
  clue returned uncut                                 0.00 %
  equal-width slices, any n, any rounding             0.00 %
  random cut positions, n random                      8.60 %   <- the blind floor
  random cut positions, n = 6 always                 13.20 %
  random cut positions, n = 5 always                 15.40 %
  "severed = n" (v1's trap)                           9.80 %   built 100 %
  "2+, a half counting only for its left slice = n"   44.20 %   built 46 %
  "slices the topping touches at all = n"            27.20 %   built 92 %
  "slices with two WHOLE pieces = n" (no halves)     33.60 %   built 34 %
  "slices with two of any one topping = n"           13.20 %   built 100 %
  "slices with two pieces of anything = n"           25.80 %   built 93 %
  "number of slices = n"                              6.20 %   built 0 %
  "number of cuts = n"                                8.60 %   built 50 %
  "slices with three or more = n"                    10.00 %   built 8 %
  "slices with none of it = n"                        6.60 %   built 100 %
  "the fullest slice holds n"                        10.00 %   built 100 %
  "slices with EXACTLY two = n"                      86.20 %   built 91 %
  demo replay (previous clue's answer)                0.00 %
  one constant answer for every clue                  0.20 %
  junk: empty / whitespace / 4000 chars / the clue    0.00 %
The payoff ladder is 9-15 % (well formed, no idea) -> 10 % (the knife family) -> 26-34 % (right family, wrong readout) -> 34-44 % (right measurement, wrong halves convention) -> 100 %. No reading that lacks the insight pays more than 15 %, which is the property that matters; the near misses pay 30-44 %, which is where a partial player should sit if the class is to average near 50 %. The one entry above 50 % is not a rival law but a SYNONYM: a player who counts "slices with exactly two, a halved piece counting for both sides" has the entire insight including the halves convention, and differs from the rule only on slices holding three or more - which is why solve() shows a slice of three in 46 % of demos. v2's equivalent row was 52.8 %; the number rose because v3's digits are 2 and 3 far more often than 1 (k=1 needs two severed pieces to keep the severed decoy dead, so it is only 2 % of clues).

SHAPE AND JUNK ATTACKS on an otherwise correct answer (250 clues): reference 100 %; trailing spaces, crust rows removed, blank lines inserted, an extra header line - all 100 % (the scorer is forgiving about form). All cuts removed, one cut missing in one row, cuts shifted by one in one row, an extra cut at the far left, a dough row deleted, a dough row duplicated, upper-cased, cheese turned to spaces, a topping moved one cell, reversed left-right, dough rows reordered - all 0.00 %. One extra cut added in the middle of every row: 16 % (that is simply another cutting, and it lands on the count about as often as a blind cutting does).

SPEED AND SIZE (20000 seeds for generate, 1000 for solve): generate mean 1.08 ms, median 0.79 ms, p99 4.3 ms, max 9.4 ms, no empty clue - it draws one tray size and its 48 sample cuttings per batch and reuses them across attempts, keeps prefix sums so one candidate cutting costs O(slices), and does the equal-cutting rejection before any sampling. solve mean 8 ms, median 8.6 ms, max 80 ms. score 0.03 ms. Sizes: scorer 379 chars (cap 512), solve 3820 (cap 5000), clue <= 224, solution <= 269. score(clue, solve(clue)) == 1 on 20000 seeds.

HOW GENERATE CHOOSES THE DIGIT. For each tray and each candidate topping it takes 48 random well-formed cuttings, histograms the count, and keeps only counts that (i) are 1-3, (ii) occur on 2-15 of the 48 cuttings (4-31 % - rare enough that blind play is a foothold, common enough that a player who has the rule finds a cutting in a few dozen tries), (iii) are not achieved by ANY equal-width cutting of that tray, and (iv) have a witness cutting that carries the demo picture of (b) with severed(x) != k. The rarest surviving count wins.

INTENDED DISCOVERY PATH. (1) The clue is the tray, so a demo-less player sends the tray back with plausible edits; bars down the picture are well formed and score ~9 %, which is the foothold that stops players concluding the grader is exact-match. (2) One demo shows the answer is the clue picture with cuts, and shows a slice with two mushrooms, one of them halved by a cut, beside a slice holding only that half. (3) The digit is small, so "two slices got two mushrooms" is pointable rather than countable-wrong. (4) The last step is the halves convention, and it is still load-bearing: the same measurement with halves not counted at all is worth 34 %, and with a half counted only for the slice holding its left part 44 % - not 100 %.

LEVERS IF IT DRIFTS. Too hard: force one of the two pieces on the counted slice to be whole (measured: costs generate 1.08 -> 1.73 ms); let the digit be 1 more often by dropping the severed-decoy requirement for k=1; widen the rarity band (raises the blind floor). Too easy: narrow the band to 2-8 of 48 (blind floor ~5 %); require the counted slice to hold nothing but that topping; go back to two named toppings (v2's clue) which puts blind play at ~3 %.
